name: Erik Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small firm, eleven of us, and nearly all our clients are charities: a hospice, two youth clubs, a refugee support group, that sort of thing. My day is year-end accounts, gift aid claims, which is the tax the government gives back to charities on donations, and a lot of answering worried treasurers by email. I like that the numbers mean something. What wears me out is chasing receipts from volunteers who keep them in a biscuit tin.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI fit in at the moment, if anywhere?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll use a chat tool to draft a polite email to a treasurer who's three months late, or to summarise a long funding agreement. I don't trust it with the actual numbers yet. My flatmate Tom works in software and he thinks I'm a dinosaur, but I'd rather see it work for a year on someone else's files first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that got oversold, and that's fine with me. I'd probably post something about how the charity sector never had money for the shiny stuff anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. Our charity clients can't afford big software, so our work would carry on like normal. The firm is steady, the partners are fair, and I'm not worried about my job in this one. The routine bits, like coding bank lines, might get a little quicker, and I wouldn't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and use the email drafting a bit more. I'd keep putting about two hundred a month aside, which gets me to roughly five months of savings by next summer. And I'd finally sit the charity finance certificate, because I want to move in-house at a charity in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. A bit flat, maybe, after all the build-up, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the charity sector never had money for the shiny stuff. Is that a worry for your clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, actually. A lot of the small ones are just about hanging on, with grants getting smaller every year. That's a worry for them more than for me, but if one of the youth clubs closes, I lose a client I really care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, I told you, it's a fancy autocomplete. Tom would say give it five years. We'd argue about it over pasta like we always do.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent tool** that got oversold.
I'd point out the **charity sector** never had money for shiny software anyway.
think: My **firm is steady** and the partners are fair, so my job feels safe.
Only **routine bank coding** gets quicker, which I'd welcome.
do: Use AI a bit more for **email drafting** to slow treasurers.
Keep saving **£200 a month** toward five months of cover.
Sit the **charity finance certificate** to move in-house later.
feel: **Calm**, if a bit flat after the build-up.
S0.quote: Our charity clients can't afford big software, so our work would carry on like normal.
fieldNote: Erik's **job security** comes from a steady, fair firm and loyal clients.
His worry is for **struggling charities**, not for himself.
Plans a **slow move in-house** at a charity regardless of AI.
Trusts AI with **words, not numbers**, a clear line for him.

steps.text: Keep preparing year-end accounts and gift aid claims for charities
Use AI more for drafting reminder emails to treasurers
Save £200 a month to reach five months of cover
Sit the charity finance certificate next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules so the savings go back into the work, not just to shareholders. At work I'd say let's be the firm that uses this well for small charities who can't afford a full-time accountant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think our firm shrinks. Gift aid claims and year-end accounts are mostly checking and form-filling, and that's exactly what this card describes. The partners wouldn't sack me overnight, but I don't think they'd replace Ruth when she retires, and I might end up doing her work plus mine for the same pay, or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for proper training on the tools, paid, in work hours, and I'd learn them properly this time. I'd move my savings target up to six months and cut the weekend trips. And I'd start applying for in-house charity finance jobs within a year, because a charity needs someone in the building who knows the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, I've got some savings and some time, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, our bookkeeper. She's 61 and she's brilliant at what she does, but what she does is coding bank lines. And our trainee, Kofi, because I'm not sure there's a second-year job for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools properly this time. What changed from the first picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the plateau one it was a nice extra. Here it's the job. If the work moves into software, I'd rather be the person who checks the software than the person the software replaced.

say: I'd say **rules** should send savings back into the work, not shareholders.
I'd pitch the firm as the one that **uses AI well** for small charities.
think: My gift aid and year-end work is **mostly checking**, exactly what goes first.
I'd likely end up doing **two jobs' work** for the same pay or less.
do: Ask the partners for **paid training** on AI tools in work hours.
Raise my savings target to **six months** and cut weekend trips.
Apply for **in-house charity finance** jobs within a year.
feel: **Anxious**, but with some savings and time to act.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who checks the software than the person the software replaced.
fieldNote: Erik shifts from **casual AI use** to learning it seriously once it's the job.
His worry centres on **colleagues**: Ruth near retirement and trainee Kofi.
Sees **in-house roles** as safer because charities need someone who knows people.
Expects **more work** for the same pay, not a sudden layoff.

steps.text: Ask the partners for paid AI training in work hours
Raise the savings target from five to six months
Cut weekend trips away to free up money
Apply for in-house charity finance jobs within a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a public response, fast: income support, training, something like a basic income while people work out what's next. I'd sign every petition and I'd say it at work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone by 2028. There's no hands-on part to accounting, so I don't get the three-year gap that a care worker would. The in-house charity job wouldn't save me either, because a charity would just use the AI too. The only things left would be the human bits, and I'm not sure anyone pays for those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop all non-essential spending and push savings past six months. I'd talk to Tom about whether we can afford to stay in the flat or move somewhere cheaper. I'd volunteer more at the food bank on Saturdays, partly to keep a reference and a foot in community work. And I'd join a union, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd worked hard for the qualification, and then someone moved the finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the human bit of your job, if any?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sitting with a hospice treasurer who's crying because the numbers don't add up is the bit of my job I'm proudest of. The auditors are coming, and I explain it calmly. I tell her it's going to be fine. I don't know if that's a job, but it matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move somewhere cheaper. Where would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back near my mum, probably, on the edge of town where rent's about a third less. I'd hate leaving the flat, but I'd rather do that than go through my savings in a year.

say: I'd call for **income support** and training, maybe a basic income.
I'd **sign petitions** and say it openly at work.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**, with no hands-on gap to buy time.
Even **in-house charity roles** would just use AI too.
do: Stop non-essential spending and push savings past **six months**.
Move somewhere cheaper, **near my mum**, if rent becomes too much.
Join a **union** and volunteer more at the **food bank**.
feel: **Frightened**, like the finish line moved after years of study.
S2.quote: Sitting with a hospice treasurer who's crying because the numbers don't add up is the bit of my job I'm proudest of.
fieldNote: Erik grasps that **pure desk work** gets no robot delay.
The emotional **human side** of his job is what he values most.
His fallback is **family and community**: mum, food bank, flatmate.
A first-time **union joiner**, pushed by speed of change.

steps.text: Stop all non-essential spending in the first month
Move near his mum where rent is a third lower
Join a union for finance workers
Volunteer more Saturdays at the food bank for references

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and we should treat it like one. I'd push our professional body to start talking about transition support now, not in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me one good move. I'd be 32 when it arrives. Probably I'd want to be in a role where I'm managing people and money together, like running a charity's operations, not just the books. Even that's thinking work, though, so I'm not fully safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the charity finance certificate this year and apply to in-house roles by 2027. I'd ask for operations work in any charity I join, things like managing volunteers and running buildings. I'd keep saving about two hundred a month and learn the AI tools properly so I'm useful in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but able to breathe. Five years feels like enough to do something sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even operations is thinking work. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. But running a charity building and a team of volunteers means being there, unlocking the hall and sorting out arguments. Those bits come later, with the robots, if they come at all. It's not perfect, but it buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom and I talked about each getting our own places in a couple of years. I think I'd stay in the shared flat longer here. It's cheaper, and having a mate around helps when things are uncertain.

say: I'd call five years a **warning** we should act on now.
I'd push our professional body on **transition support** before 2030.
think: Five years gives me **one good move**, at 32.
Charity **operations work** mixes people and buildings, buying some time.
do: Pass the **charity finance certificate** this year.
Apply for **in-house roles** by 2027, asking for operations duties.
Keep saving **£200 a month** and learn AI tools properly.
feel: Five years feels like **enough time** to act sensibly.
S3.quote: Running a charity building and a team of volunteers means being there, unlocking the hall and sorting out arguments.
fieldNote: Erik uses the **robot delay** cleverly: operations has hands-on parts.
He'd **stay in shared housing** longer as a cushion.
His plan is the **same direction** as before, just sooner.
Still sees **no full safety**, so stays anxious.

steps.text: Pass the charity finance certificate this year
Apply for in-house charity roles with operations duties by 2027
Keep saving £200 a month in the shared flat
Learn the AI accounting tools properly at the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want our firm to plan openly with staff, so nobody gets surprised in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine for a long while. I'd be 37 when it arrives, and by then I'd hope to be running a charity's finance and operations, maybe even as a director. My bookkeeping work goes, but the people work might hang on, and I'd have years to build savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm another two years, then move in-house. I'd keep learning the tools as they arrive, slowly. I'd also start a pension top-up, a small one, because ten years of normal life means I should still plan for being 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit of worry in the background, like weather on the horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your trainee Kofi in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to go into charity work properly, not just the numbers. Learn to run a team and talk to funders, because that's where the human parts are. And use the AI tools from day one, so he's not starting late like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a pension top-up. Isn't that odd if AGI is coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But if I've learned anything from my clients, it's that you don't know. A hospice that thought it would close in 2020 is still going, so I'd rather have a bit of money put by.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** not to waste.
I'd want the firm to **plan openly** with staff.
think: By 37 I'd hope to be a charity **finance and operations** lead.
My **bookkeeping** goes, but the people work might hang on.
do: Stay at the firm **two more years**, then move in-house.
Learn the AI tools **slowly**, as they arrive.
Start a **small pension top-up** for later life.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with worry in the background.
S4.quote: A hospice that thought it would close in 2020 is still going, so I'd rather have a bit of money put by.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Erik follow his **existing plan** at an easy pace.
His **pension top-up** shows he hedges against uncertainty, not just AGI.
Still expects his **bookkeeping** to vanish, so worry remains.
His advice to Kofi centres on **people skills**.

steps.text: Stay at the charity firm for two more years
Move in-house to a charity finance and operations role
Learn new AI accounting tools as they arrive
Start a small monthly pension top-up

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. What would help is a proper income floor while people retrain, and funders giving charities money for staff, not just for software.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how I'd feel about the charities themselves. If everything goes digital, some of these tiny groups lose the one person who understood their money. That worries me almost more than my own job.

headlineQuote: I'd worked hard for the qualification, and then someone moved the finish line.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old** accountant at an eleven-person firm serving **charities**.
He shares a flat with Tom and uses AI **for words, not numbers**.
He calls for **rules and income support**, and worries for vulnerable clients.
Across the pictures, his escape is an **in-house charity role** mixing people and operations.
His mood rises from **calm** in the plateau to **alarmed** with AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because accounting has no hands-on gap to buy time.
whatWouldHelp: Funders giving charities money for **staff, not software**.
